name: Who Pays: The Hidden Cost of Privatized Credit
deck: Affirm's 48% Q3 2026 GMV growth shows consumer installment credit escaping regulated banking, while institutional investors in private credit and alternative funds pay carried-interest fee loads (headline 2-and-20; mega-funds actually 1.25-1.5% plus 20% carry, Callan buyout mean 1.74%) on products that public mutual funds deliver for 40 basis points. The burden cascades invisibly: pension funds lose 15-30% of gross returns to fee drag, small businesses face a record 15.8% default rate in the lower-middle-market as private credit stretches to reach them, and infrastructure users pay it directly—American Fork, Utah sewer bills rose 100%+ over four years, MTA tolls jumped 7.5% in January 2026.
core_bet: Private-capital colonization extracts costs from three groups in order of visibility. Retail investors and institutional limited partners pay explicit fee premiums (2-and-20 on private credit funds vs. 40-50 basis points on public mutual funds) for products that often underperform public indices even before fees. Bank customers and small businesses lose access to relationship-based lending as capital flows toward higher-return private assets; prime borrowers get captured by alternative operators at low spreads, forcing banks either to raise spreads on subprime borrowers or exit entirely. Communities lose the credit infrastructure that once served SMBs, creating a secondary market for predatory lending and making small-business formation harder. Affirm's explosive growth (48% GMV in Q3 2026, 146% Affirm Card growth, $36.7B FY2025 GMV) shows that even consumer credit—traditionally the most visible and regulated form of lending—is now being captured by alternative-finance operators that operate outside banking regulation but enjoy similar capital access through venture funding.

mechanism: The cost structure of private-capital colonization is buried in three layers, each making the burden invisible to the final customer. At the surface, institutional investors (pension funds, endowments, wealth managers) allocate capital to private-credit funds and alternative-asset managers. The advertised '2-and-20' is largely a myth at scale—mega-funds like Apollo, Blackstone, and KKR charge 1.25-1.5% management fees, and the Callan 2024 study of 413 partnerships found a buyout mean of 1.74%. But the total load is worse than the headline suggests: carry is rising through stepped 15%/20%/25-30% tiers tied to MOIC, and 100% of funds in the Callan dataset offset management fees with transaction and monitoring fees charged directly to the portfolio companies (an offset that shows up as higher prices for the companies' customers). The Callan study's blunt conclusion: private-equity fees have 'not come down over time.' For equivalent credit exposure, public credit mutual funds charge 40-50 basis points, and fee drag removes 15-30% of gross MOIC—turning a 3.0x gross fund into roughly 2.0-2.2x net to pension beneficiaries. Affirm exemplifies the same cost shift in consumer credit: it raises capital from venture investors at implied valuations that assume it captures merchant-funding spreads, interest income from installments, and card-linked fees. Traditional banks, subject to deposit-insurance regulations and liquidity requirements, cannot pay those implied returns. So capital systematically flows toward Affirm even though it finances the same consumer transactions a bank could finance.

Beneath that visible fee layer is a credit allocation problem. When capital flows into private credit seeking 12-15% returns, it competes for the same borrowers (SMBs, real estate, consumer installment) that banks once financed at 6-8% spreads. Private-credit managers and alternative operators bid up prices for the highest-quality credit (Affirm focuses on 'near-prime' and 'prime' consumers; Blackstone and KKR infrastructure funds target investment-grade assets), leaving banks with lower-quality borrowers, forced either to raise spreads (making credit more expensive for vulnerable borrowers) or to exit the market entirely. Loews owns CNA, an insurance company with float that can be deployed into credit strategies; that float itself is cheaper capital than deposits due to tax and regulatory arbitrage, allowing Loews to outbid traditional banks for the same credit. The result is a bifurcated credit market: prime credit flows to private capital operators at low spreads, while subprime or relationship-dependent credit (small businesses that need a loan officer's judgment, or consumers with thin credit histories) gets either more expensive or disappears—and the strain shows up as a record 6.0% private-credit default rate reported by Fitch by April 2026, with small borrowers under $25M EBITDA defaulting at 15.8% versus 4.0% for large ones. When a PE firm acquires an infrastructure asset, it often finances the deal with private-credit debt at leverage a local operator cannot access: Blackstone's $6B+ Enverus buyout (August 2025) layered on $3.4B of private-credit debt at 8.5x EBITDA (SOFR+500-550bps), and its $2.5B Champions Group HVAC/plumbing deal (February 2026) went in at 18.5x EBITDA with over $1B of private credit at SOFR+450bps. Not every deal is debt-loaded—Blackstone's $11.5B TXNM Energy utility acquisition (May 2025) was explicitly all-equity with no new leverage, showing the model varies by asset—but the pattern of using capital-markets access to bid away assets that banks and municipalities once held is consistent.

The final layer is systemic. When credit creation moves from regulated banks (which must maintain capital buffers, pass stress tests, and limit leverage) into private-equity-backed operators and alternative funds (which operate in a lighter regulatory envelope), credit supply becomes more procyclical. In good times, private capital floods into credit, driving explosive growth (Affirm's 48% GMV growth). In downturns, private capital withdraws or gets hamstrung by LP redemptions and mark-to-market losses, and credit collapses faster than the traditional banking system would allow. Communities and small businesses—lacking the scale to access capital markets—bear the brunt of that collapse. The burden of supporting credit availability shifts from regulated banks (where capital requirements force some continuity of lending) to private operators (who can exit instantly). This shift is visible in infrastructure fees that pass the burden of capital returns and rising debt-service costs directly to end users. American Fork, Utah's Timpanogos sewer district raised bills 40% in January 2024, 15% in 2025, and another 15% planned for January 2026—over 100% cumulative in four years. Toll authorities are compounding annual increases: the Pennsylvania Turnpike raised tolls 5% (2024), 5% (2025), and 4% (January 2026); New York's MTA imposed a 7.5% toll increase alongside a subway fare bump to $3.00 in January 2026; and the Port Authority of NY/NJ layered a 3% January 2026 rise on top of a $0.25/axle annual escalator running through 2028. These escalators—often locked into CPI-plus formulas at acquisition or concession—outpace the 1-2% increases typical under direct municipal control, and they compound every year regardless of the asset's actual cost trend.
why_now: Three shifts have accelerated privatization in 2024-2026, and the deal record shows the money moving in real time. First, regulatory pressure post-2008 made traditional banking less profitable, pushing capital toward less-regulated alternatives; private-credit AUM has now reached $1.9 trillion, with 2024 fundraising of $197-233B (across just 188 funds, the lowest count since 2011) and roughly $240B in 2025—capital consolidating into fewer, larger vehicles like KKR's $6.5B Asset-Based Finance Partners II and Coller's $6.8B Credit Opportunities II (both 2025). Second, asset managers recognized credit is a profitable intermediate layer if you source capital cheaply and avoid regulated-bank costs; infrastructure debt deal volume jumped from $790B (2024) to $1.05 trillion (2025), up 33% year over year. The named take-privates are large and recent: KKR's $5.7B Integer Holdings CDMO deal (August 2026, 14x EBITDA, the largest CDMO take-private ever), KKR's $4.75B CoolIT exit to Ecolab at 29x NTM EBITDA (a ~15x return in two years on an AI-data-center-cooling asset), and Carlyle selling $18B of assets in 2025 (against a $4-5B target) including the $7.2B Medline IPO, the largest US PE-backed IPO ever. Third, technology made origination frictionless: Affirm's AdaptAI and BoostAI systems underwrite in real time without loan officers; its $36.7B FY2025 GMV shows capital can build consumer-credit supply with none of the traditional bank infrastructure. The inflection is urgent because regulatory windows are closing—after SVB and the 2023 bank failures, capital and liquidity rules are tightening on banks, pushing still more credit creation into the lightly regulated alternative channel just as its default cracks (Fitch's record 6.0% private-credit default rate by April 2026) start to show.
who_pays: Four groups carry the burden, each in a way the others cannot see. **Pension beneficiaries and retail savers** pay through fee drag that removes 15-30% of gross returns. The '2-and-20' they think they escaped is not the real cost: even where mega-funds charge 1.25-1.5%, the Callan 2024 study of 413 partnerships found a buyout mean of 1.74% and concluded fees have 'not come down over time,' while stepped carry tiers (15%/20%/25-30% by MOIC) and 100% use of portfolio-company monitoring-fee offsets push the total load higher. Concretely, a fund that returns 3.0x gross nets a pension beneficiary only about 2.0-2.2x—the missing turn is transferred to the manager. Academic work (Begenau & Siriwardane, Journal of Finance 2024) found 5.8 percentage points of carry variance for different LPs in the same fund, so smaller pensions systematically pay more than large ones for identical exposure. **Small-business owners** pay through both scarcity and default risk being priced back onto them: as prime credit flows to private capital, lower-middle-market borrowers (under $25M EBITDA) now default at 15.8%—nearly four times the 4.0% rate for large borrowers—and roughly 65% of 2025 defaults were 'soft' amend-and-extend or PIK-toggle restructurings that defer stress rather than resolve it, with over 70% of eventual hard defaults following within two years. The small borrower gets credit, but at terms that quietly transfer the downside risk back to them. **Infrastructure users and communities** pay the most visible bill. American Fork, Utah residents saw sewer rates rise 40% in January 2024, 15% in 2025, and another 15% set for January 2026—over 100% in four years. Pennsylvania Turnpike drivers absorbed 5%, 5%, and 4% increases across 2024-2026; New York MTA riders got a 7.5% toll increase and a $3.00 subway fare in January 2026; Port Authority NY/NJ layered 3% onto a per-axle escalator running through 2028. These compound annually under CPI-plus concession formulas, far above the 1-2% typical of direct municipal control. **Consumers with thin credit histories** pay through exclusion: Affirm concentrates on near-prime and above (65%+ of its US approvals presented as 0% APR to the most creditworthy), leaving the subprime consumer to OppFi, Elevate, or payday lenders at 400%+ APR—a segment venture-backed BNPL has vacated and has no incentive to undercut.
who_profits: Private-capital operators (Affirm, private-equity-backed credit platforms, alternative-asset managers, infrastructure fund sponsors) capture the value, and the general partner captures it twice—once in management fees, again in carry on the spread. Affirm's Q3 2026 adjusted operating income was 27% of revenue, a margin traditional banks cannot match after capital requirements, FDIC insurance, and compliance costs. Loews profits by deploying CNA insurance float (cheaper than deposits due to regulatory arbitrage) into strategies that out-yield Treasuries, posting $1.7B net income in 2025. The clearest windfalls are in the exits: KKR bought CoolIT Systems for $270M in June 2023 and sold it to Ecolab for $4.75B in March 2026 at 29x NTM EBITDA—roughly a 15x gross return in under three years, on which the GP takes 20%+ carry. Carlyle's Q3 2025 distributions hit $21.5B, five times the prior quarter, and it sold $18B of assets against a $4-5B target. The chain moves from pensioners and savers (who pay the fees and absorb the drag) to GPs and top LPs (who collect the carry). Infrastructure sponsors compound it further: a 1.25-1.5% fee on AUM, plus carry on exit, plus the portfolio companies' own fee income—the toll escalators and sewer-rate increases that ratepayers pay every year—all accrue to the fund. The smaller LPs, meanwhile, pay measurably more carry than the anchor investors for the same fund (5.8pp of documented variance), so even inside the winners' circle the burden is tiered.
tension: The tension is unsustainable fee compression. If private-credit funds outperform and LP demand stays high, fee pressure eases. But Affirm's profitability depends on capital remaining cheap, origination staying frictionless, and credit losses staying low. A recession, rising capital costs, or credit tightening at scale all threaten the economics. Moreover, regulatory scrutiny will eventually reach private credit: once policymakers notice that $15T+ of non-bank credit creation is happening outside regulated banking, pressure will mount for either regulatory capture or capital restriction. The secondary tension is credit allocation: if private capital siphons all the good credit, the banking system becomes a residual holder of bad credit, raising systemic fragility. A stress scenario: if prime credit dries up during a recession (private capital redemptions force asset sales), small businesses cannot access credit at any price, and systemic credit contraction is sharper than if credit had remained in regulated banks. Finally, the LP fee dynamic creates a transparency problem: pension funds and retail investors may not realize they are paying 2-and-20 for credit exposure that public funds offer for 40 bps. Regulatory scrutiny on private credit fee transparency is rising: the SEC has flagged concerns about fee disclosure in private fund prospectuses, and California's pension system (CalPERS) has publicly complained about private-credit fee loads and J-curve returns drag.
surprising_part: The most surprising fact is that Affirm Card GMV grew 146% in Q3 2026 while core BNPL growth plateaued—the real profit is not one-time purchase financing but a payment network with repeat usage and card-linked economics, a bank-like system that is harder to regulate and more profitable than the BNPL thesis suggested. The secondary surprise cuts against the easy narrative: the '2-and-20' most critics attack does not actually exist at scale. Mega-funds charge 1.25-1.5%, and the Callan study puts the buyout mean at 1.74%. The extraction is real but hides in less-scrutinized places—the stepped carry tiers that quietly rise with MOIC, the monitoring fees charged to portfolio companies (used by 100% of funds in the Callan set), and the 5.8-point carry gap between big and small LPs in the very same fund. The burden isn't a single headline number; it's a set of offsets and tiers designed to be individually defensible and collectively opaque. And the sharpest surprise for the leverage thesis is a counterexample: Blackstone's $11.5B TXNM Energy utility deal (May 2025) was explicitly all-equity with no new debt—proof that the fee-and-tier extraction, not leverage alone, is the durable mechanism.
one_sentence: Private capital colonizes credit creation by capturing high-quality borrowers at low spreads while leaving regulated banks with residual, lower-return portfolios—and passing the fee costs to pensioners, the cost of credit to small businesses, and infrastructure fee increases to communities.
societal_stake: If credit creation increasingly flows outside regulated banking, the public loses the stability that regulation provides: capital buffers, stress-testing, and mandatory lending continuity. In downturns, credit withdraws faster than the traditional banking system would allow, hitting small businesses and communities hardest. Pensioners and savers lose real returns to fee extraction that benefits alternative managers and operators. Infrastructure users face higher fees to service PE acquisition debt and LP distributions. And the credit-allocation system becomes more bifurcated: prime borrowers get cheap capital from alternative funds, while subprime and relationship-dependent borrowers get either excluded or served by increasingly predatory lenders filling the gap left by traditional banking. Over a 20-30 year horizon, this bifurcation creates two credit systems: one for the capital-markets-connected, one for everyone else—and the gap widens as regulation tightens on traditional banking.
